plan.contextChunk: This figure plots the probability simplex for a three-class problem on a set of three-dimensional coordinate axes. The axes are black arrows radiating from a shared origin: y_1 runs to the right, y_2 runs straight up, and y_3 runs down and to the left toward the viewer. Each axis carries a single tick labeled 1, and each unit point is annotated with a bold class name, Car at y_1 equal to 1, Bike at y_2 equal to 1, and Bird at y_3 equal to 1. A translucent pink triangle is filled in with its three corners resting exactly on those unit points, and the stretches of axis inside the triangle are drawn darker where the shading passes over them. The slanted face, not the volume it cuts off, is what carries the meaning: only points on that plane are admissible, the geometric form of requiring three nonnegative scores that sum to one. The drawing accompanies the definition of a classifier as a mapping from RGB images into the (K-1)-dimensional simplex, here with K equal to 3, where each vertex is an unambiguous prediction of one class and interior points are graded mixtures.

elements: shared origin where the three axes meet
y1 axis: black arrow from origin pointing screen-right (+X), extending to ~1.5 with arrowhead
y2 axis: black arrow from origin pointing straight up (+Y), extending to ~1.5 with arrowhead
y3 axis: black arrow from origin pointing down-left toward the viewer (+Z), extending to ~1.5 with arrowhead
tick mark labeled '1' on each axis at the unit point
axis-end labels y1, y2, y3 in italic serif
bold class label 'Car' at the y1 unit point (1,0,0)
bold class label 'Bike' at the y2 unit point (0,1,0)
bold class label 'Bird' at the y3 unit point (0,0,1)
translucent pink triangle (the simplex face) with corners exactly at the three unit points
darker maroon axis segments from the origin to each unit point, drawn where the shading passes over them
draggable probability point (small sphere) constrained to the triangular plane
live readout labels for y1, y2, y3 (and their sum = 1) shown near the point or in a corner HUD

interactions.teaches: Dragging the point anywhere on the pink triangle changes y1, y2, y3 while their sum stays exactly 1 — a classifier's output is a constrained mixture, not three independent numbers; only points on this plane are admissible predictions.

Clicking a vertex label (Car, Bike, or Bird) snaps the point to that corner and drives the other two coordinates to zero, showing that a vertex is an unambiguous single-class prediction with probability 1.

interactions.label: Prediction
interactions.teaches: Stepping through the named states moves the point between the interior (a graded, uncertain mixture) and each vertex (a confident, one-hot decision), making the geometry of certainty visible.

demo_steps.title: Graded mixture
demo_steps.narration: The point sits inside the triangle at roughly (1/3, 1/3, 1/3): the classifier is uncertain and spreads its confidence across Car, Bike and Bird. Every interior point is a valid prediction because the three scores are nonnegative and sum to 1.

demo_steps.title: Snap to Car
demo_steps.narration: Selecting Car moves the point to the y1 vertex: y1 = 1 while y2 = y3 = 0. A corner of the simplex is a fully confident, unambiguous prediction of a single class.

demo_steps.title: Snap to Bird
demo_steps.narration: Selecting Bird moves the point to the y3 vertex (down-left toward the viewer): now y3 = 1 and the others vanish. Each vertex corresponds to exactly one class label.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale ~1.5 units. Axes from origin: y1 = +X (screen-right), y2 = +Y (screen-up), y3 = +Z (receding diagonal drawn down-left toward viewer); each axis line length ~1.5 with arrowhead, tick + '1' label at the unit point. Simplex triangle vertices: Car (1,0,0), Bike (0,1,0), Bird (0,0,1); fill translucent pink #f4b6ad at ~0.55 opacity, double-sided. Axis segments from origin to each unit point drawn darker maroon #6b1f1f (linewidth larger) on top of the black axes to mimic the source's shaded-over look. Axis lines/arrowheads and y1,y2,y3 labels black #111111; class labels bold black. Draggable point: sphere radius ~0.06, color #d62828, always on plane x+y+z=1. Readout HUD shows y1,y2,y3 to 2 decimals plus 'sum = 1.00'. Constraint: barycentric coords clamped to [0,1] so the point never leaves the triangle.
interactionPlan.notes: On drag, raycast the pointer onto the plane x+y+z=1, convert the hit to barycentric coordinates w.r.t. the three unit-point vertices, clamp each to [0,1] and renormalize so the sum is exactly 1, then place the sphere at the clamped barycentric position and refresh the readouts. Clicking a class label (or choosing the button state) tweens the sphere to that vertex (coord=1, others=0); free dragging sets the button state back to 'Mixture'. Render the pink triangle with a DoubleSide MeshBasicMaterial and depthWrite false so the darker inner axis segments remain visible through it. Keep the standard isometric pose so y1 reads right, y2 up, y3 down-left, matching the source.

discrepancies: Camera angle differs: source has y3 axis going steeply down-left (~45° below horizontal) while generated figure uses a more symmetric ~30° oblique view, making the triangle appear more equilateral than in the source
Red draggable point at the centroid (1/3,1/3,1/3) is present in the generated figure but absent from the source
The pink triangle appears more symmetric/equilateral in the generated view versus the more elongated appearance in the source due to the different projection angle
evaluation.notes: All core elements (axes, arrowheads, tick marks, maroon segments, pink simplex triangle, class labels) are correctly implemented with meaningful drag and snap-to-vertex interactions; the main weakness is a slightly different camera angle that makes the triangle appear more equilateral than the source's more elongated oblique view.
action_items: Adjust the camera view to use a steeper angle for the y3/z-axis (e.g. axisScreenAngles z: 45-50) so the triangle appears more elongated like the source figure
Consider hiding the red point by default or making it smaller so the initial view more closely matches the source
